title: Add new neutral return-value option to window.confirm?

labels.name: needs implementer interest
labels.description: Moving the issue forward requires implementers to express interest

body:
Talking with @avidrissman, I think we should explore having a 3rd return value for `confirm` that indicates "the User did not choose an option in the dialog".  Eg. we see if we can get away (from a web compat perspective) with changing it from returning `boolean` to `boolean?`

Use cases:

1. Some browsing environments just have no way to display such a dialog.  For example when in VR headset mode, Chrome cannot show confirm dialogs.
2. To prevent abuse and avoid event-loop lock-ups Chrome [now auto-dismisses](https://developers.google.com/web/updates/2017/03/dialogs-policy) confirm dialogs when you switch tabs, returning `false`.
3. To further prevent abuse we'd like to experiment with not showing confirm dialogs at all for background tabs.

In all such cases we could return `false`, but IMHO not giving developers any reliable way to distinguish between a dismissed dialog and the user clicking cancel violates the [transparency principle for interventions](https://github.com/wicg/interventions#intervention-design-guidelines).  Eg. I could imagine a banking site being upset that their "Your session is about to timeout, press OK to close or Cancel to remain on the page" dialog now leads to users staying logged-in indefinitely without their knowledge, and they have no great way to fix this without changing the behavior for when the tab is visible.  Note that I don't think the page visibility API is sufficient - it doesn't necessarily (at least in Chrome) have all the same context around OS window stacking order/occlusion that some mechanism to auto-dismiss dialogs would.

One nice thing about using `boolean?` is that `null` will probably get treated the same as `false` in most code today.  Of course there are almost certainly going to be some cases where that's not true and `null` causes breakage, so we're going to have to study the web compat implications before we know for sure if this makes sense.  But I wanted to get the discussion started to see if doing the experiment is even worthwhile.

I don't see any other obvious options.  I guess we could introduce `maybeConfirm` which behaves exactly like `confirm` but with the `null` and `false` treated separately if we wanted to make differentiating the cases 100% opt-in (but if we were going to do that, would we be better off just adding a `confirmAsync` that returns a promise?).

@domenic WDYT?

If this doesn't sound totally crazy to people then we could write a spec PR and try shipping it in Chrome and consider landing this only after that's proven successful from a web compat perspective.
